primer.eur_p_world.title: Christendom
primer.eur_p_world.text: You were born in Latin Christendom — Europeans simply call it "Christianity". Above kings and princes stand two supreme powers, the pope in Rome and the Holy Roman Emperor, who forever argue over which is greater. The land is divided among lords: a vassal receives a fief from his lord — land with its peasants — and serves for it with his sword. The language of the Church, the law and scholars is Latin, while at home people speak dozens of tongues.
primer.eur_p_world_1000.title: After the year 1000
primer.eur_p_world_1000.text: The second millennium since the birth of Christ has begun. France is ruled by the Capetians, though the king's power barely reaches beyond the lands around Paris; Germany by the Saxon emperors and, from 1024, the Salian ones. In 1054 Rome and Constantinople broke communion; in 1066 Duke William of Normandy conquered England; and in 1077 Emperor Henry IV stood for three days in a penitent's shirt at the castle of Canossa, begging forgiveness from Pope Gregory VII.
primer.eur_p_world_crusades.title: The age of crusades
primer.eur_p_world_crusades.text: This is the age of the crusades. In 1095 Pope Urban II at Clermont called for the liberation of the Holy Sepulchre, and in 1099 the crusaders took Jerusalem. Towns are growing, buying charters of liberties from their lords, and Gothic cathedrals rise where old churches stood — the first was the choir of Saint-Denis (1144). England is ruled by the Plantagenets: Henry II, under whom Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170, and Richard the Lionheart.
primer.eur_p_world_high.title: The high Middle Ages
primer.eur_p_world_high.text: The Middle Ages are at their height. Pope Innocent III (1198–1216) sits in judgement over kings; in 1215 the English barons forced King John to seal the Magna Carta; and universities bustle in Paris, Oxford and Bologna. King Louis IX of France, Saint Louis, builds the Sainte-Chapelle to house Christ's crown of thorns. There are more Europeans than ever before — so many that in 1315–1317 endless rains and failed harvests brought the Great Famine.
primer.eur_p_world_plague.title: Plague and the Hundred Years' War
primer.eur_p_world_plague.text: A grim century. In 1347 Genoese ships brought plague from Crimea, and within four years the Black Death killed, by estimates, a third to a half of all Europeans; then it returns again and again. Since 1337 England and France have been fighting a war that will later be called the Hundred Years' War, and in 1429 a peasant girl, Joan of Arc, lifted the siege of Orléans. From 1378 the Church has two popes at once, later three, and the schism lasts until 1417.
primer.eur_p_world_print.title: The printing press
primer.eur_p_world_print.text: The world is changing before your eyes. Around 1455 in Mainz Johannes Gutenberg printed a Bible with movable type, and printed books spread across Europe by the thousand. In 1453 the Turks took Constantinople, and Greek scholars carry their manuscripts to Italy. In England the houses of Lancaster and York fight for the crown in the Wars of the Roses, and in 1492 the Genoese Columbus, sailing Castilian ships, reached unknown lands across the ocean.
primer.eur_p_world_florence_commune.text: Florence is a commune — a city that governs itself. There is no king: power lies with the Signoria, priors chosen from the guilds for just two months, and the Ordinances of Justice of 1293 barred the noble magnates from office altogether. The city is torn by the feud of Guelphs and Ghibellines, then of "Whites" and "Blacks" — that is how the poet Dante was exiled in 1302. And in 1378 the Ciompi, the day-labouring wool carders, rose up and held power for several weeks.
primer.eur_p_world_florence_medici.title: The Medici
primer.eur_p_world_florence_medici.text: On paper Florence is a republic, but since 1434 the Medici bankers have ruled it from behind the scenes: Cosimo the Elder, then his grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent. Their money pays Donatello, Botticelli and the young Michelangelo, and over the city rises Brunelleschi's cathedral dome — the largest in the world, built without wooden centring. In 1478 the Pazzi conspirators tried to murder the Medici at Mass in the cathedral, and after 1494, when the Medici were driven out, the preacher Savonarola thunders in the city.
primer.eur_p_world_toledo.title: City of Castilian kings
primer.eur_p_world_toledo.text: In 1085 King Alfonso VI of Castile took Toledo from the Muslims, and the ancient Visigothic capital became a city of the Castilian kings. Christians, Jews and Muslim Mudéjars live side by side, and under King Alfonso X the Wise (1252–1284) scholars of three faiths translate Arabic books and write laws in Castilian. But tolerance is fading: in 1391 anti-Jewish riots swept Castile, and in 1492 Isabella and Ferdinand expelled every Jew who would not accept baptism.
primer.eur_p_society.title: Three orders
primer.eur_p_society.text: Learned monks say society has three orders: those who pray, those who fight and those who work. At the top are the king, dukes and counts; below them knights, who receive a fief from their lord and swear loyalty kneeling, their hands placed between his. The clergy, from bishop to village priest, live on the tithe. But most people are peasants, and in the towns a new kind of folk is growing: merchants and guild masters. A runaway serf who lives in a town for a year and a day often becomes free.
primer.eur_p_society_serf.title: Serfs
primer.eur_p_society_serf.text: You were born into a family of serfs. You are not slaves: you cannot be sold one by one, and you have your own house and strip of land, but you are bound to your lord's soil and cannot leave, marry outside his manor or make your son a priest without his leave. Several days a week you labour on the lord's fields, you pay dues, and when the head of the family dies the lord takes the best cow or ox. Freedom can be bought, or won by running away to a town.
primer.eur_p_society_peasant.title: Free peasants
primer.eur_p_society_peasant.text: Your family are free peasants: you are not bound to the land and may leave, but you pay your lord a rent for your holding — in coin, grain, hens at Christmas and eggs at Easter. The village farms by three fields: one sown with winter wheat or rye, one with oats and peas, the third lying fallow. You also pay to grind at the lord's mill and bake in the lord's oven — the banalités — and every tenth sheaf of the harvest, the tithe, goes to the Church.
primer.eur_p_society_noble.title: Those who fight
primer.eur_p_society_noble.text: Your family is among those who fight. At about seven a boy is sent as a page to a lord's household, then becomes a squire, and at around twenty he is dubbed a knight with a blow of the hand or a sword on the shoulder. You live in a stone castle or fortified manor; your wealth is land and peasants, your honour lies in loyalty to your liege. A warhorse, mail and sword cost as much as a whole herd of cows, so knighthood is an expensive business. Daughters are married off for alliances and land.
primer.eur_p_birth.title: Baptise without delay
primer.eur_p_birth.text: Children are born at home with a midwife and the neighbour women; men are kept out of the room. The baby is baptised as soon as possible, often on the very first day: one who dies unbaptised, it is believed, cannot be buried in consecrated ground, and if the newborn is weak the midwife may baptise it herself. The godparents give the name — usually a saint's or their own: John, Peter, William, Mary, Agnes. The mother stays away from church for about forty days and is then "churched" with a prayer of thanksgiving.
primer.eur_p_childhood.title: Before seven and after
primer.eur_p_childhood.text: Until seven a child is simply a child: swaddled tight, breastfed for about two years, playing with a ball made of a pig's bladder, spinning tops, clay whistles, stilts and wooden horses. At seven real life begins: peasant children herd geese and gather firewood, craftsmen's sons are apprenticed to a master for about seven years, and a few go to a church school to learn Latin. Children are loved, though people quote the Bible: "He that spareth his rod hateth his son."
primer.eur_p_home.title: Hearth and thatch
primer.eur_p_home.text: A peasant house has one or two rooms of wattle and daub under a thatched roof. In the middle is an open hearth with no chimney — smoke drifts out through the thatch — and in winter the cow and hens live behind a partition, warming the house. The whole family sleeps on straw mattresses. In towns houses are timber-framed, two or three storeys high: a shop or workshop below, and upper floors jutting over the narrow street, where slops are thrown out. Fire is the townsfolk's greatest fear.
primer.eur_p_food.title: Bread and ale
primer.eur_p_food.text: The main food is bread — a labourer eats about a kilogram a day — with a thick pottage of peas, beans and cabbage, cheese and eggs. People drink ale in England and Germany, wine in France, Italy and Castile. Peasants eat meat on feast days, nobles almost daily: game, pork, pies spiced with pepper and saffron. On Fridays and in Lent meat is forbidden, so everyone eats herring — salted, smoked or dried.
primer.eur_p_clothes.title: Broadcloth and pointed shoes
primer.eur_p_clothes.text: Peasants wear a linen shirt, a knee-length woollen tunic, a hood and wooden clogs or leather shoes. Townsfolk and nobles dress in brightly coloured Flemish and Florentine broadcloth: costly scarlet is dyed with kermes, a dye made from insects. Sumptuary laws forbid commoners to wear ermine and silk. By the fourteenth century tight jackets, long-toed poulaines and tall headdresses for women come into fashion. Married women always cover their hair.
primer.eur_p_faith.title: To the sound of bells
primer.eur_p_faith.text: The faith is Catholic, and all life moves to the sound of bells: they mark the hours of prayer, call people to Mass and toll for the dead. Mass is said in Latin and few understand the words, but everyone knows the Our Father and the Hail Mary. At least once a year, at Easter, one must confess and take communion. Pilgrims travel to relics — in Rome, Canterbury, Santiago de Compostela — and every saint has a speciality: Saint Nicholas protects children, Saint Apollonia cures toothache.
primer.eur_p_faith_jewish.title: The Jewish community
primer.eur_p_faith_jewish.text: You come from the Jewish community. Jews live in their own quarters — in Cologne, Paris, London — around the synagogue, the mikveh bath and the cemetery, under the protection of the king or archbishop, for which they pay heavy taxes. You are barred from owning land or joining guilds, so many trade and lend money at interest, which the Church forbids to Christians. Community life is fragile: in 1096 crusaders massacred Jews along the Rhine, and later Jews were expelled from England (1290) and France (1306, 1394).
primer.eur_p_faith_toledo_jewish.title: The Jews of Toledo
primer.eur_p_faith_toledo_jewish.text: You belong to the Jews of Toledo, one of the largest and most learned communities in Europe. Your physicians, translators and tax farmers serve the kings of Castile, and around 1357 Samuel ha-Levi, treasurer to King Pedro I, built a synagogue with carved walls in Moorish style — later called El Tránsito. But after the riots of 1391 many were baptised — they are called conversos, "the converted" — and in 1492 the unbaptised were given four months to leave Castile.
primer.eur_p_faith_muslim.title: The Mudéjars
primer.eur_p_faith_muslim.text: You are a Mudéjar, one of the Muslims who stayed on under the kings of Castile. Alfonso VI promised to leave you your mosques and laws, and though Toledo's Great Mosque was soon turned into a cathedral, your communities live on, with their own alfaquíes — scholars of the law — and their own judges. Mudéjars are the finest masons, carpenters and potters: their carved ceilings and brick towers adorn churches and synagogues alike. But you pay special taxes and live in your own quarter, the morería.
primer.eur_p_work.title: Guilds and fairs
primer.eur_p_work.text: Nearly everyone works the land. In towns craftsmen join guilds — weavers, bakers, smiths — which watch over quality and prices, keep outsiders out and celebrate their patron saints' days. An apprentice lives with his master for about seven years, then becomes a journeyman, and a master only after making a "masterpiece", a model piece of work. Merchants gather at the fairs of Champagne, trading Flemish cloth for Italian spices, and silver deniers and pennies are minted by almost every great lord.
primer.eur_p_work_florence.title: Wool and florins
primer.eur_p_work_florence.text: Florence lives on wool and money. The Calimala guild finishes and resells imported cloth, while the Lana guild runs hundreds of workshops employing thousands of carders, spinners and weavers. Since 1252 the city has minted the florin, a gold coin of 3.5 grams accepted from London to Cairo. Bankers — the Bardi, the Peruzzi, later the Medici — sit at their benches, the banchi, lend money to kings and popes and keep their accounts in double entry.
primer.eur_p_place.title: Forests, fields and bell towers
primer.eur_p_place.text: Europe is forests, fields and endless villages with a church tower in the middle, with lords' castles and monasteries in between. Towns are small: most have a few thousand people, and only the largest — Paris, Venice, Florence — reach a hundred thousand or so. Every town has a wall and gates locked at night, and the roads are bad: pilgrims trudge along them, merchant carts rumble by, and robbers lie in wait.
primer.eur_p_place_paris.title: City on the Seine
primer.eur_p_place_paris.text: Paris is the largest city north of the Alps: by 1300 it has, by estimates, over 200,000 people. On the Île de la Cité stand the royal palace and Notre-Dame, begun in 1163 and nearly a century in the building. The Right Bank belongs to merchants, the Les Halles market and the Seine wharves; the Left Bank is the Latin Quarter, where university students speak Latin and brawl with the townsfolk. King Philip II Augustus ringed the city with a wall and had the main streets paved.
primer.eur_p_place_london.title: City on the Thames
primer.eur_p_place_london.text: London stands on the Thames inside its old Roman walls. To the east rises the White Tower, built by William the Conqueror; to the west, Westminster Abbey and the royal palace. A single bridge crosses the river — London Bridge, of stone since 1209, with houses and shops built right on it. The citizens are proud of their liberties and their mayor, the fishmongers' and drapers' guilds are rich, and Cheapside smells of bread, ale and leather.
primer.eur_p_place_florence.title: City on the Arno
primer.eur_p_place_florence.text: Florence lies on the Arno among Tuscan hills of vineyards and olive groves. Stone towers of noble families jut above the cramped streets — once there were more than a hundred — and the Ponte Vecchio, lined with butchers and tanners, spans the river. The air smells of wool and dye works, and the Arno sometimes runs blue and scarlet. Florentines call their city the daughter of Rome and are proud of the poet Dante, who wrote not in Latin but in their own Tuscan tongue.
primer.eur_p_place_cologne.title: Holy Cologne
primer.eur_p_place_cologne.text: Cologne is the largest city in Germany — "holy Cologne", with dozens of churches and monasteries. Since 1164 it has kept the relics of the Three Magi, brought from Milan, and for them a huge Gothic cathedral was begun in 1248 — it will not be finished before the Middle Ages end, and a wooden crane stands on it for years. Cologne merchants trade Rhine wine and cloth from London to Novgorod, and in 1288 the citizens defeated the archbishop's army at Worringen and have been free in all but name ever since.
primer.eur_p_place_toledo.title: City on the rock
primer.eur_p_place_toledo.text: Toledo stands on a rock almost encircled by the river Tagus. Narrow winding lanes, brick towers in Moorish style, synagogues, mosques and churches side by side. Since the twelfth century translators have worked here: Christians, Jews and Muslims together render Aristotle, Ptolemy and Ibn Sina from Arabic into Latin. Toledo smiths are famous for blades of tempered steel, and since 1226 a Gothic cathedral has been rising on the site of the Great Mosque.
primer.eur_p_law.title: Lords' courts and ordeals
primer.eur_p_law.text: Everyone has their own court: peasants are judged by their lord, clergy by church courts, townsfolk by their own judges under the town charter, and nobles by the king or their peers. Truth is sought through witnesses and oaths, and sometimes by ordeal — hot iron or water; in 1215 the Lateran Council forbade priests to take part. Knights settle disputes by combat. Punishments are fines, the pillory, banishment, and for grave crimes the gallows that stand outside every town.
primer.eur_p_health.title: Doctors and relics
primer.eur_p_health.text: The rich call a physician trained at Salerno or Montpellier in Galen and Ibn Sina: he holds urine up to the light and lets blood. The poor go to the barber, the herb woman or the relics of the saints. Monasteries and towns keep hospitals for the poor, pilgrims and the sick, and outside the walls leper houses for lepers. Fevers, dysentery and "Saint Anthony's fire" — ergot poisoning from rye bread — are dangerous, and from 1347 plague, returning every ten or fifteen years.
primer.eur_p_women.title: Wife, widow, abbess
primer.eur_p_women.text: Girls marry at about 15 to 20 — noble girls earlier — and the Church requires the consent of both: without the bride's "yes" the marriage is invalid. A wife runs the house, spins, brews ale and works in the fields; in town she helps in her husband's workshop and may run her own trade — Paris and Cologne even have women's guilds of silk spinners. A widow controls her own share of property. Universities and offices are closed to women, but convents are not: the abbess Hildegard of Bingen wrote on medicine, music and her visions.
primer.eur_p_leisure.title: Carnival and tournaments
primer.eur_p_leisure.text: The year is full of holidays: Sundays and dozens of saints' days are days off. At Christmas people sing and feast for twelve days, before Lent they revel at carnival, in May they raise the maypole and dance, and on Midsummer Eve they light bonfires. Jugglers, puppeteers and travelling players with mystery plays on Bible stories perform in the squares. People play dice, chess and a ball game fought over by whole villages, while nobles hunt with falcons and hold tournaments.
primer.eur_p_knowledge.title: Latin and universities
primer.eur_p_knowledge.text: Few can read — mostly clerics. Schools in monasteries and cathedrals teach the seven liberal arts: grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music. By the thirteenth century universities have grown up in Bologna, Paris and Oxford, where students spend years hearing lectures in Latin and arguing in disputations. Books are copied by hand on parchment and one can cost as much as a house; only after the 1450s does the printing press make them cheap.
primer.eur_p_war.title: Knights and archers
primer.eur_p_war.text: The main force in war is the heavy knight on a warhorse, in mail and later in plate armour. But fortresses decide everything: stone castles are besieged for months. Kings fight over inheritances and land, and knights go on crusade — to the Holy Land, to Spain, to the Baltic. In the Hundred Years' War English longbowmen cut down French knights at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415), and by the fifteenth century cannon begin to smash castle walls.
